F = G * (m1 * m2) / r^2 [1]

m1 = earth mass (or black hole mass)

m2 = your mass

G = gravitational constant

r = distance between gravitational attachment point(aka middle of the blackhole, and your centre of mass)

It is like replacing the sun with a black hole with the mass of the sun. Nothing will change.

[1] wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitation

Something will change. Let's say you're on a hypothetical platform above black hole about 6000km away. Then all the mass that's attracting you is directly below you which means that all the mass attracts you with foll force.

However, in case of Earth, not all the mass is directly below you. Some of the mass wants to pull you diagonally in both directions and a very small amount wants you to pull you almost sideways towards both directions as well. This means that the combined directional gravity has to be lower on Earth. If Earth's density was uniform rather than the densest part being at the center, the difference would be bigger.

Grospoliner is correct - you can crank your way through multiple integrals if you want to prove it to yourself, but the long and short of it is that the different locations cancel each other out.

For every kilogram of mass that's closer to you than the center point, there's a kilogram that's farther away. For every kilogram that's off-center, there's a kilogram that's opposite it.

You can treat the gravity of any spherical homogeneous body as being a single point of mass at its center, with one caveat: if you're inside the sphere then the shortcut no longer works.

It would be exactly the same. The gravity from an extended object that you're outside of is exactly the same as if all that mass would be concentrated in a point. The thing that makes black holes so gravitationally agressive is not their mass but their density. The gruesome effects happen when you get close to the black hole itself. If you dig into the Earth, the layers above you won't attract you anymore, so you end up with less and less mass below you to pull you down, until you become weightless at the center. For a black hole, that attraction keeps going up as you get closer to the event horizon.

It's proximity to high-density mass that tears you apart, not the mass itself.
But if you'd compare gravity of surface of Earth with hypothetical Earth-mass and Earth-sized hollow sphere with shell being only 5 kilometers thick, would you tell the difference?

Purely from a single point gravitational measurement, if we assume that all of these are perfectly spherical? No, there'd be no way to tell the difference.

Of course, tidal forces also occur, and the tidal forces from the Sun and the Moon will clearly tell you if a planet has a hollow, solid or liquid interior.
